title: Sh-L-M
hookLine: shalom, shalem (whole), shilem (paid): peace means wholeness
last: TALMUD, STUDENT, TEACHER: ONE ROOT, LEARNING.

cards: A receipt stamped paid. A coffee mug with no chips in it. A man limping home after a long, hard night, finally arriving in one piece.
And a greeting used coming in and going out. In English they have nothing in common. In Hebrew, the same three letters: shin, lamed, mem.
A few days ago you read shalom letter by letter and stopped there. Today we lift out the root, and it turns out to be bigger than the word you thought you knew.

teach.b: Sh-L-M. Four ways in. First, shalem: whole, complete, nothing missing.
In Deuteronomy, a merchant is told to keep a weight that is shelemah, whole, and tzedek, just: no shaving a little off when the customer isn't looking. A whole weight is an honest one.
Second, shilem: to pay, to make good.

teach.h: SHILEM: PAY IT BACK, MAKE IT WHOLE.
teach.b: In the laws of Exodus, when someone damages what belongs to a neighbor, the Hebrew says he must make it whole, with a verb from this root: restitution, paying it back until nothing is missing. Third, the man limping home.
In Genesis, after Jacob wrestles all night and leaves limping, after he meets the brother he feared, the text says he arrived shalem at the city of Shechem.

The commentator Rashi reads it three ways: whole in his body, healed; whole in his possessions, even after the gifts he gave away; whole in his learning, having forgotten nothing in his long years away. Fourth, shalom.
Read through its root, peace isn't only the absence of a fight.
It's wholeness: nothing owed, nothing broken, nothing missing.

A home at peace is a home where things are whole between people. When people greet each other with shalom, they may be wishing far more than quiet. Paying what you owe is one way of making something whole.

how: Jewish teaching connects shalom, peace, with shalem, whole, and the laws of the Torah require paying back what was damaged or borrowed; shalom is also the everyday greeting and a word that closes many prayers.

o: the root of shalom: whole, complete, paid
the root of Shabbat: rest, stopping, ending
the root of shema: hearing and listening

s: in Hebrew, peace and payment share a root
shalom and shilem both grow from shin, lamed, mem.
shalom only means that nobody is fighting
its root says whole: nothing owed, nothing broken, nothing missing.
Rashi reads Jacob's arrival as whole in body, possessions and learning
three kinds of whole, after a hard road home.

games.q: you're a merchant in Deuteronomy, and a slightly light weight would earn a little more. what does the text ask for?
o: a light one, if nobody checks.
games.why: a weight that is shelemah, whole, and tzedek, just. whole and honest turn out to be close neighbors.

practice: Let your mind look for one small thing still open: a text you owe a reply, a little money borrowed from a friend, a book never returned, a thank you you meant to say.
Hold it and notice how it sits, slightly unfinished, then breathe in and feel what whole might be like. If you pray, you can hold that one thing in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Sh-L-M. Shin, lamed, mem: the root of shalom, peace; shalem, whole; and shilem, paid. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: whole, complete, from the same root as shalom.

carryVoice: Your line: peace is wholeness. Paying back can be a kind of peace. That's today, done.
